nameStory: The lancet clubtail gets its name from the unique shape of the male's claspers - the appendages at the tip of his abdomen used for mating. These claspers are shaped like a lancet, which is a sharp, pointed surgical instrument that doctors once used for making small cuts. It's like nature gave this dragonfly its own tiny medical tools!
description: The lancet clubtail is a medium-sized dragonfly that's part of the clubtail family, known for their club-shaped abdomens that widen at the tip. At about 1.7 inches long, it's roughly the size of your thumb. This handsome dragonfly sports a black body decorated with bright green stripes along its thorax (the middle section) and green triangular markings down its abdomen. The last two segments of its abdomen flash cheerful yellow patches along the edges, like tiny warning lights.

idTips.label: Green thorax stripes
idTips.description: Look for bright green stripes running lengthwise down the thorax (chest area) - they stand out boldly against the black background and catch the light beautifully when the dragonfly turns

idTips.label: Green abdominal triangles
idTips.description: The abdomen displays distinctive green triangular markings that look like little arrowheads pointing toward the tail - these geometric patterns are quite striking and regular

idTips.label: Yellow tail patches
idTips.description: The last two segments near the tip of the abdomen show bright yellow patches along the outer edges - they look like tiny yellow racing stripes on an otherwise dark tail

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: About thumb-sized at 1.7 inches long with the typical clubtail body plan - relatively sturdy thorax tapering to a narrower abdomen that widens again at the tip

idTips.label: Male claspers
idTips.description: Males have distinctively lance-shaped claspers at the tail tip that look like tiny pointed tools - you'll need to get close or use binoculars to see this detail clearly

habitat: Lancet clubtails prefer rivers and larger streams with moderate to fast-flowing water, especially areas with sandy or rocky bottoms. You'll often spot them perched on rocks, logs, or bare ground near the water's edge, as clubtails love to bask in sunny spots. They're less common around still ponds and prefer waterways with some current movement.

seasonality.spring: Adults haven't emerged yet - the nymphs are still developing underwater in rivers and streams, growing slowly in the cold water.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight season runs from June through July when adults are actively flying, mating, and laying eggs. This is your best time to spot them perched near flowing water or patrolling their territories.
seasonality.fall: Adult flight season has ended and eggs are developing in the water. The new generation exists as tiny nymphs beginning their underwater development phase.
seasonality.winter: Nymphs continue their slow development underwater, breathing through gills and hunting small aquatic prey while waiting for warmer weather to trigger their emergence.

funFact: Lancet clubtail nymphs are incredible underwater predators that can shoot out their lower lip like a spring-loaded harpoon to snatch prey - this extendable jaw can extend nearly half their body length in a fraction of a second, making them the underwater equivalent of a chameleon catching flies!
confusionNotes: The lancet clubtail can be tricky to distinguish from other clubtails in the same genus, especially the dusky clubtail and ashy clubtail. The key memory trick: remember 'lancet = green triangles' - the distinctive green triangular markings on the abdomen are your best field mark, as the other similar species have different patterns or colors in their abdominal markings.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name Phanogomphus is relatively new in dragonfly classification - many field guides from before 2017 will list this species under the old genus name Gomphus. Don't be confused if you see it listed as 'Gomphus exilis' in older resources - it's the same species, just with updated scientific naming based on recent genetic research.
compareHints: Among its Phanogomphus relatives, the lancet clubtail is distinguished by its bright green thorax stripes and green triangular abdominal markings. The beaverpond clubtail has more yellow coloring and prefers still water, while the dusky clubtail is generally darker with less prominent green markings. The ashy clubtail lives up to its name with more grayish coloration rather than the lancet's vibrant greens.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Phanogomphus relatives in New England, the Beaverpond Clubtail is most reliably identified by habitat - it strongly prefers beaver ponds and similar still waters over the flowing streams favored by Rapids and Lancet Clubtails.
Among its Phanogomphus relatives, the dusky clubtail lives up to its name with more subdued coloration than the bright yellow Rapids Clubtail or the pale Ashy Clubtail.

Among its Phanogomphus cousins, the Ashy Clubtail is distinguished by its pale coloration — the Dusky Clubtail is much darker, the Rapids Clubtail has more distinct yellow markings, and the Lancet Clubtail is smaller and more delicately built.
Among its Phanogomphus relatives in New England, the harpoon clubtail is distinguished by its specific tail appendage shape and the pattern of yellow markings on its thorax.
